problems.stem: A frame shows an animation of cell division while the narrator reads, word for word, the full paragraph of text already printed on the same screen. Which principle does this violate?
options: The personalization principle, because the tone is too formal.
The redundancy principle, because identical on-screen text and narration force the learner to process the same words in two channels.
The pre-training principle, because key terms were not defined.
No principle; reading the text aloud always helps.
problems.explanation: Verbatim on-screen text plus narration is redundant and splits the visual channel between the animation and the text. Narrate over the visual, or show the text, but not both saying the same words.

problems.stem: A designer converts a multi-row reference table of conversion factors into audio-only narration, citing the modality principle. Why is this a misapplication?
options: Audio is always lower quality than text.
Reference content that learners must inspect and re-check belongs as durable text; transient audio forces re-listening and overloads memory.
The modality principle applies only to children.
Tables can never be narrated.
problems.explanation: The modality benefit assumes transient, learner-paced explanatory content alongside a graphic. Reference or complex material that must be re-inspected is better as text the learner can scan.

problems.stem: An AI tool offers to auto-add narration to a frame that already has dense on-screen text over a busy diagram. What design judgment must you apply before accepting?
options: Accept it, since more channels always means more learning.
Recognize that modality offloads words to audio so the eyes can read the graphic; stacking text, audio, and a busy image overloads rather than offloads.
Accept it only if the narrator voice is female.
Reject all AI narration on principle.
problems.explanation: The modality principle works by moving words off the crowded visual channel. Keeping the text and adding narration on top of a busy diagram defeats the purpose and overloads both channels.

problems.stem: You decide narration over animation is the right modality for a process frame. To make the decision defensible across your learner population, what must accompany the narration?
options: A louder default volume.
A synchronized caption or transcript, so learners who are deaf, hard of hearing, or in audio-off contexts still get the content.
A faster playback option only.
Nothing; narration alone is sufficient.
problems.explanation: A modality choice is only defensible when it includes an equivalent. Captions or a transcript keep the audio channel from gating access for part of the audience.

problems.stem: A learner leaves a 'confusion' annotation with low confidence on a frame that swapped narration for printed text. Their revision changed only the font and text size. Which combination of signals should drive the next adaptive move?
options: The completion status: the frame was finished, so advance to the next section.

The note type plus the revision quality: a confusion annotation with low confidence and a cosmetic-only revision shows the modality logic was never addressed, so the system should explain or re-represent the principle.
The font choice: better typography would have resolved the confusion.
The confidence score alone: low confidence always means more practice items.
problems.explanation: Adaptive support reads the combination of the annotation type, the artifact evidence, confidence, and revision quality. Here the confusion note plus a polish-only revision (font and size, not the narration-versus-text decision) signals the learner has not engaged the modality principle itself, so the right move targets the reasoning, not the styling.
